Forecasting the population dynamics of disease vectors is critical for mitigating the risks of vector‐borne diseases under a changing climate. We evaluate an iterative Bayesian forecast model of black‐legged tick ( Ixodes scapularis ) phenology and population dynamics at near‐term to interannual (e.g., 12‐month) scales. The black‐legged tick is the vector of Borrelia burgdorferi , the causative agent of human Lyme disease. Our forecasts outperformed a seasonal null model during peak questing periods when disease risk is highest. The null model was based on historical day‐of‐year averages. Iterative data assimilation improved forecast performance over time, demonstrating the ability to adaptively learn about climate‐driven shifts in demographic parameters, and reinforcing the value of long‐term data to support management. Effective management of recovering large carnivores depends on monitoring systems that are accurate, scalable, and cost‐efficient. This need is particularly acute in Europe, where rapid wolf recolonization is creating new challenges for management and policy. Individual identification, on which conventional monitoring often relies, can be costly and logistically demanding, but for social carnivores the reproductive unit can be a more practical and management‐relevant target. Building on this, we conducted systematic winter camera trap surveys between 2015 and 2023 at 102 fixed sites in the Western Swiss Alps and characterized gray wolf recolonization dynamics without individual identifications. Wildfires are becoming more extensive and extreme in many parts of the world, and these changes to fire regimes are a threat to many plant and animal species. After the 2019–2020 Australian megafires, the most extensive forest wildfires globally at that time, multiple studies were funded to evaluate the impacts of the fires on biodiversity. We gathered 62 datasets, predominantly presence/absence or abundance data, collected (1) from the same sites before and after the fires, (2) from burnt and unburnt sites after the fires, or (3) using an unplanned before‐after‐control‐impact design. We curated these into a single dataset and used available data layers to generate consistent site‐level covariates across projects, including those related to location, fire history, ecosystems, climate and land use. Rapid evolution of defense strategies in non-native plants contributes greatly to their invasion success. Many studies have evidenced reduced resistance in non-native plants following specialist herbivore release, but how these plants adjust their defense portfolio against generalist herbivores in the introduced range remains poorly understood. Using the widespread plant invader Spartina alterniflora as a model species, we systematically compared three defense strategies against generalist herbivores-constitutive resistance, induced resistance, and tolerance-among its three genetic groups (native populations, high-, and low-latitude introduced populations) in a common garden. Modeling species distributions in dynamic pelagic environments remains challenging, particularly for wide-ranging and highly mobile species when there is limited guidance on model performance. This limitation constrains the effective use of species distribution models (SDMs) in marine conservation, where robust and transferable predictions are essential for conservation planning. Using the loggerhead turtle (Caretta caretta) as a case study, we developed a benchmarking workflow to compare modeling strategies across spatial resolutions, environmental predictor variables, and algorithms. Climate change and land-use changes are key drivers of global biodiversity loss. Many species are shifting to higher elevations or latitudes in response to global warming, often encountering unfavorable land-use conditions during the shift. However, existing approaches often lack spatial flexibility, overlook shape and size constraints, or rely on limited environmental parameters, reducing their effectiveness in real-world applications. Antarctica is designated as a natural reserve devoted to peace and science, with Antarctic Specially Protected Areas (ASPAs) serving as the primary instrument for area-based biodiversity protection. However, the existing ASPA network lacks the comprehensiveness and representativeness required under Annex V, Article 3(2), of the Madrid Protocol. We demonstrated the application of systematic conservation planning to explore the trade-offs underlying protection at a continent-wide scale, focusing on the principles of comprehensiveness and representativeness. These principles are the foundations of designing an effective protected area system that ensures all biodiversity features and their diversity are captured. Cascade dam development is transforming freshwater ecosystems worldwide, yet the long-term responses of fish beta diversity to progressive hydrological disturbances remain poorly understood. We analyzed data from the upper reaches of the Yellow River on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau spanning five decades (pre-1975 to 2023), across a 1983-km river corridor influenced by sequential cascade dams. We quantified temporal shifts in taxonomic, phylogenetic, and functional beta diversity and determined the contributions of species extinctions and introductions to multidimensional beta-diversity change. Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis ( Bd ), the causative agent of chytridiomycosis, is one of the most significant emerging infectious pathogens affecting amphibians worldwide. Despite Brazil harboring the greatest amphibian diversity on planet, a comprehensive assessment of the occurrence patterns of Bd across the country remains lacking. A total of 5,539 Bd -positive individuals were compiled, encompassing 204 amphibian species distributed across multiple Brazilian ecoregions. Asymmetric colonisation patterns often arise from large‐scale biotic exchanges involving two source areas. In the Pliocene, the closure of the isthmus of Panama facilitated the admixture between North and South American faunas, an event termed Great American Biotic Interchange (GABI). The ecological mechanisms underlying the asymmetry of the GABI, incontestably in favour of North American lineages, remain debated. Here, coupling a mechanistic eco‐evolutionary simulator with palaeoclimatic reconstructions, we test fundamental hypotheses relating this biogeographic imbalance to palaeoclimate dynamics. When climate is the only constraint to species' dispersal, our simulations yield more South‐to‐North than North‐to‐South dispersal events, mostly within the tropical biome. Mammals continue to face increasing extinction risk, largely driven by escalating human pressures. However, the drivers of change in extinction risk remain poorly understood. We used an ordinal modeling framework (cumulative link mixed models) to test the correlation between biological traits, ecological characteristics, anthropogenic threats, and trends over time to analyze changes in extinction risk for 4,992 mammal species assessed by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List of Threatened Species. Since 1996, most species remained stable, but extinction risk increased by ∼9% and decreased for <1% of the mammals. Evaluating the response of plant species to climate change and predicting changes in their potential distributions are crucial for developing effective species conservation and management strategies. Oreorchis patens, a widely distributed orchid species in the northern temperate zone, is an important component of the temperate orchid flora due to its strong cold resistance, unique summer dormancy characteristics and strong asexual reproduction ability. In this study, six species distribution models were constructed based on the Biomod2 package. By comparing the parameters, the optimized MaxEnt model was finally used to predict the potential suitable habitat of O. patens within a five-country study areas in East Asia, which will be of great significance for the biodiversity conservation of this orchid species. item.title: Migration strategy and colonization: the disproportionate role of partial migration
item.description:
相关度 72.0 · 提出部分迁徙者更易定殖新区域，可解释分布与预测全球变化下的定殖物种

Colonization drives diversification and determines how species shift their ranges, making it central to ecology and evolution. As both seasonal migration and dispersal depend on locomotor capacity, migration could be a major yet overlooked route to colonization. Here, we present evidence that partially migratory species are disproportionately successful in founding new populations, whereas strict migrants establish more rarely despite routinely reaching potentially suitable habitat in novel areas. Building on the threshold model of migration, we propose that partial migrants’ liability to migrate lies closer to the threshold and/or is more environmentally sensitive, allowing displaced individuals to settle. This mechanism can help explain species distributions and diversification and predict which species might colonize newly suitable areas under global environmental change.

Tropical‐origin invasive plants are increasingly expanding towards higher latitudes. Two well‐recognized strategies can facilitate this process: evolving enhanced cold tolerance or phenological adjustment that enables reproduction within a shortened growing season. However, whether plants can coordinate these strategies to facilitate poleward range expansion remains largely unknown. We reconstructed the 109‐year invasion history of Ageratum conyzoides (Asteraceae) in China using historical distribution records. To assess cold adaptation, we quantified cold tolerance and its physiological and biochemical basis through common‐garden experiments across six populations spanning the species' latitudinal invasion gradient. We compared two geographically distant populations of the invasive dipteran Psychoda albipennis (Maritime Antarctica and the Magellanic sub-Antarctic) to assess population-level variation in lower and upper thermal tolerance. Urbanization poses various threats to bird populations worldwide, of which bird‐window collisions (BWCs) contribute to a significant proportion of human‐related bird mortalities. Due to regional biases in collision research and a lack of model systems for identifying multi‐scale drivers and vulnerable species, little is known about the impact of collisions on European bird populations and the effects of various ecological factors on collision rates at larger scales. Here, we used long‐term ringing‐encounter data from Finland's national bird monitoring scheme to identify the vulnerability of Finnish bird species to BWCs and predict spatiotemporal dynamics of BWCs across the country. The Asiatic cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus venaticus), once widespread, now survives only in Iran, with its population nearing extinction. In this study, we synthesised 13 years (2012 to 2024) of monitoring data to assess demographic and spatial patterns of this critically endangered subspecies in Iran. Using extensive camera trap surveys across eight reserves, supplemented by published records of cheetah occurrences on social media, we identified 24 adult cheetahs in the Northern and Southern Landscapes. No reproduction or new individuals have been recorded in the Southern Landscape for over a decade, while the Northern Landscape supports the remaining population, likely fewer than 30 adult individuals. Climatic niche metrics can improve climatic impact assessments by accounting for species‐specific climatic requirements. The species–area relation (SAR) has been extensively studied over the past century, yet the sources of variation around an estimated SAR curve remain poorly understood. Here, we show that the sampling variance of the SAR can be decomposed into two additive components: 1) conditional variance, assuming that regional richness is fixed and represents uncertainty associated with local sampling; and 2) an additional component attributable to uncertainty in regional species richness, including uncertainty arising from rare species that remain undetected in the regional sample.
